lessons.title: Fence materials, tools and safety
lessons.html:
Fence materials, tools and safety

Fences keep animals in the right camp, keep stock off roads and protect crops from animals. A good fence saves the farm money and prevents accidents.

Materials

  • Straining posts: strong posts at the ends, corners and gates. They carry the pull of the wire. They need stays (braces) to stop them leaning.
  • Line posts: wooden poles or steel Y-standards placed in a straight line between the straining posts.
  • Droppers: thin wood or steel pieces between posts that keep wires apart.
  • Wire: plain (smooth) wire, barbed wire, or mesh such as bonnox for sheep and goats.
  • Tie wire: thin wire to fix the line wires to posts and droppers.

Tools

  • Fencing pliers, wire cutters and a wire strainer (monkey strainer).
  • Spade, crowbar and post-hole digger.
  • Standard driver for steel posts.
  • Tape measure and a long string line.

Safety

Fencing can cause serious injuries. Wire under tension can whip back and cut your face or eyes.

  • Wear leather gloves, safety glasses, long sleeves and boots.
  • Never stand in line with a wire that is being strained. Stand to the side.
  • Do not over-strain wire. Follow your supervisor's instructions for tension.
  • Carry barbed wire on a bar through the roll, not against your body.
  • Lift heavy posts with two people and bend your knees.
  • Use the standard driver with both hands and keep your fingers away.
  • Pick up all cut wire pieces. Animals can get caught or swallow them.
  • Never work on or near an electric fence unless it is switched off and you have been told it is safe.

lessons.title: Building and maintaining the fence
lessons.html:
Building and maintaining the fence

Building a new fence

  1. Mark the line. Put a peg at each end and pull a string line tight between them.
  2. Clear the line. Remove bushes and stones along the fence line.
  3. Plant the straining posts. Dig the holes deep, stand the posts upright and ram the soil in firmly in layers. Fit the stays.
  4. Put in the line posts. Follow the string. Space them evenly at the distance your supervisor gives you.
  5. Run out the wire. Roll the wire along the line. Do not let it kink.
  6. Tie the wire to one straining post. Wrap it around and tie off firmly.
  7. Strain the wire. Use the wire strainer at the other end. Pull until the wire is tight but not over-strained. Stand to the side.
  8. Tie off and fix. Tie the wire to the second straining post and to each line post at the right height.
  9. Fit droppers between posts so the wires stay evenly spaced.

Start with the bottom and top wires, then do the wires in between. Keep the bottom wire close to the ground so small animals cannot crawl under.

Maintaining fences

Walk or drive along fences regularly, especially after storms, floods and veld fires. Look for:

  • broken or slack wires;
  • leaning or rotten posts;
  • gaps under the fence where water has washed soil away;
  • missing droppers;
  • branches lying on the fence.

Repairing a broken wire

  1. Pull the two ends together with the strainer.
  2. Join them with a strong knot, such as a figure-of-eight join, or a joining sleeve.
  3. Re-tension and tie to the posts again.

Write down what you repaired and report big problems, like a washed-out river crossing, to your supervisor.

Key points

  • Straining posts with stays carry the pull of the wire.
  • Use a string line so the fence is straight.
  • Never stand in line with wire being strained; wear gloves and safety glasses.
  • Check fences regularly, especially after storms and fires.
  • Pick up loose wire so animals are not hurt.
